stem: An alternating voltage is given by \( e = 6 \sin (100\pi t) \). find (i) the peak value (ii) frequency (iii) time period and (iv) instantaneous value at time \( t = 2 \) ms
solution:
\( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \)
\( e = 6 \sin (100\pi t) \)
(i) Comparing the two equations, the peak value of the alternating voltage is \( e_0 = 6 \) V
(ii) \( \omega t = 100\pi t \quad \therefore 2\pi f t = 100\pi t \)
Frequency \( f = \frac{100\pi}{2\pi} = 50 \) Hz
(iii) Time period \( T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50} = 0.02 \) s
(iv) The instantaneous value of the voltage at \( t = 2 \times 10^{-3} \) s is
\( e = 6 \sin 100\pi \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 3.527 \) V

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: An alternating voltage given by \( e = 140 \sin 3142\, t \) is connected across a pure resistor of 50 \( \Omega \). Find (i) the frequency of the source (ii) the rms current through the resistor.
solution:
Given
\( e = 140 \sin 3142\, t \)
\( R = 50\ \Omega \)
i) On comparing with \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \)
We get \( \omega = 3142 \), \( e_0 = 140 \) V
\( \omega = 2\pi f \quad \therefore f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{3142}{2 \times 3.142} = 500 \) Hz
(ii) \( e_0 = 140 \) V
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{140}{\sqrt{2}} = 98.99 \) V
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{99.29}{50} = 1.98 \) A

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: An inductor of inductance 200 mH is connected to an AC source of peak emf 210 V and frequency 50 Hz. Calculate the peak current. What is the instantaneous voltage of the source when the current is at its peak value?
solution:
Given
\( L = 200 \) mH \( = 0.2 \) H
\( e_0 = 210 \) V
\( f = 50 \) Hz
Peak Current \( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{X_L} = \frac{e_0}{2\pi f L} = \frac{210}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.2} \)
\( \therefore i_0 = 3.342 \) A
As in an inductive AC circuit, current lags behind the emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), so the voltage is zero when the current is at its peak value.

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: 4. A Capacitor of 2 \( \mu \)F is connected to an AC source of emf \( e = 250 \sin 100\pi t \). Write an equation for instantaneous current through the circuit and give reading of AC ammeter connected in the circuit.
solution:
Given
\( C = 2\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \) F
\( e_0 = 250 \) V
\( \omega = 100\pi \) rad/sec
The instantaneous current through the circuit
\( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( = \omega C e_0 \sin \left( \omega t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( = 3.142 \times 2 \times 10^{-4} \times 250 \sin \left( 100\pi t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( = 0.1571 \sin \left( 100\pi t + \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
Reading of the AC ammeter is
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 0.707\, i_0 = 0.707 \times 0.1571 \)
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 0.111 \) A

stem:
A 100 mH inductor, a 25 \( \mu \)F capacitor and a 15 \( \Omega \) resistor are connected in series to a 120 V, 50 Hz AC source. Calculate
(i) impedance of the circuit at resonance
(ii) current at resonance
(iii) resonant frequency
solution:
Given
\( L = 100 \) mH \( = 10^{-1} \) H
\( C = 25\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 25 \times 10^{-6} \) F
\( R = 15\ \Omega \)
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 120 \) V
\( f = 50 \) Hz
(i) At resonance, \( Z = R = 15\ \Omega \)
(ii) \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{120}{15} = 8 \) A
(iii) \( f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142\sqrt{10^{-1} \times 25 \times 10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{9.9356 \times 10^{-3}} \)
\( \therefore f = 100.6 \) Hz

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: A coil of 0.01 H inductance and 1 \( \Omega \) resistance is connected to 200 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Find the impedance of the circuit and time lag between maximum alternating voltage and current.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working ends \(\Delta t = 4.019\ \text{s}\), dropping a factor of \(10^{-3}\). Its OWN expression is correct — \(\dfrac{72.35 \times \pi}{180 \times 2\pi \times 50} = \dfrac{72.35}{18000} = 4.019 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}\) — so only the final numeral is wrong. It is self-refuting: on a 50 Hz supply one full cycle lasts \(0.02\) s, so a lag of 4.019 s would be 201 complete cycles. The derivation above has been corrected to \(4.019 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}\).]

Given
Inductance \( L = 0.01 \) H
Resistance \( R = 1\ \Omega \)
\( e_0 = 200 \) V
Frequency \( f = 50 \) Hz
Impedance of the circuit \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} \)
\( = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( 2\pi f L \right)^2} \)
\( = \sqrt{(1)^2 + (2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.01)^2} \)
\( = \sqrt{10.872} = 3.297\ \Omega \)
\( \tan\phi = \frac{\omega L}{R} = \frac{2\pi f L}{R} = \frac{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.01}{1} = 3.142 \)
\( \phi = \tan^{-1}(3.142) = 72.35^\circ \)
Phase difference, \( \phi = \frac{72.35 \times \pi}{180} \) rad
Time lag between maximum alternating voltage and current
\( \Delta t = \frac{\phi}{\omega} = \frac{72.35 \times \pi}{180 \times 2\pi \times 50} = 4.019 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s} \)

stem:
A 100 \( \Omega \) resistor is connected to a 220 V rms, 50 Hz supply
(i) What is the rms value of current in the circuit?
(ii) What is the net power consumed over a full cycle?
solution:
Given
\( R = 100\ \Omega \), \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 220 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz
(i) \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{220}{100} = 2.2 \) A
(ii) Net Power Consumed
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_{\mathrm{rms}} \cdot i_{\mathrm{rms}} \)
\( = 220 \times 2.2 = 484 \) W

stem:
A sinusoidal voltage of peak value 283 V and frequency 50 Hz is applied to a series LCR circuit in which \( R = 3\ \Omega \), \( L = 25.48 \) mH and \( C = 796\ \mu \)f. Find
i) The impedance of the circuit
ii) The phase difference between the voltage across source and the currents
iii) The power factor
iv) The power dissipated in the surface
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working divides by the resistance where the impedance belongs. The rms current in a series LCR circuit is \(i_{\text{rms}} = e_{\text{rms}}/Z\), not \(e_{\text{rms}}/R\); the book substitutes \(\dfrac{283}{\sqrt{2} \times 3}\) using \(R = 3\ \Omega\) and prints \(8008.9\) W. With its own \(Z = 5\ \Omega\) the average power is \(P = \dfrac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}}\dfrac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}Z}\cos\phi = 4805\) W — the printed value is exactly \(Z/R = 5/3\) times too large, which is what identifies the mechanism. Cross-checked by \(i_{\text{rms}}^2 R\), which returns the same 4805 W. The derivation above has been corrected. Two further printing slips in the same example do NOT affect its numbers and are preserved: it writes \(X_C = 1/(2\pi f L)\) where \(C\) belongs (the substitution correctly uses \(C\)), and \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_c - Y_c)^2}\) where \(Y_c\) should be \(X_L\).]

Given
\( e_0 = 283 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz, \( R = 3\ \Omega \),
\( L = 25.48 \times 10^{-3} \) H, \( C = 796 \times 10^{-6} \) F
\( X_L = 2\pi f L = 2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 25.48 \times 10^{-3} = 8\ \Omega \)
\( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f L} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 796 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{0.2501} = 4\ \Omega \)
Therefore \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_c - Y_c)^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + (8-4)^2} = 5\ \Omega \)
Phase difference \( \phi \) is given by
\( \tan \phi = \frac{X_L - X_c}{R} = \frac{8-4}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \)
Therefore, \( \phi = \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{4}{3} \right) = 53.1^\circ \)
Thus the current lags behind the voltage across the source by a phase angle of \( 53.1^\circ \)
Power factor \( = \cos \phi = 0.6 \)
Power dissipated in the circuit
\( P_{\mathrm{av}} = e_{\mathrm{rms}}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos \phi \)
\( = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}}\, \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}Z}\, (0.6) \)
\( = \frac{283}{\sqrt{2}}\, \frac{283}{\sqrt{2} \times 5}\, 0.6 \)
\( = 4805\ \text{W} \)
